title: Fairness in Serving Large Language Models
one_line: VTC is a fair-queueing scheduler for LLM serving that keeps a per-client virtual token counter, always admits the request of the least-served client into the continuously-batched running set, and lifts a returning client's counter to the active minimum, giving a provable 2x-tight bound on the service difference between backlogged clients while staying work-conserving.

repo.evidence: The paper's abstract itself states 'The reproducible code is available at https://github.com/Ying1123/VTC-artifact' (paper.txt:48-49); the GitHub owner Ying1123 is first author Ying Sheng; repo/README.md:1 is titled 'VTC Artifact for "Fairness in Serving Large Language Models"' and repo/fair_bench/README.md:1 is headed 'Instructions for Artifact Evaluation'. The tree contains the real system (slora/server/router/vtc_req_queue.py and siblings, the full S-LoRA/LightLLM engine, workload generators and all plot scripts), not a placeholder.
repo.badge_evidence: none found - the USENIX presentation page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher and web search surfaced no badge listing; repo/fair_bench/README.md:1 ('Instructions for Artifact Evaluation') suggests the artifact went through AE but does not evidence a specific badge

H1_open_repo.evidence: Official per paper.txt:48-49 and repo/README.md:1. Contains the actual implementation: VTC scheduler at slora/server/router/vtc_req_queue.py (counter lift :44-50, least-counter selection :104-141, per-decode-step charge :144-152), the prediction variants (vtc_pred_len_req_queue.py, vtc_oracle_req_queue.py), all baselines (req_queue.py=FCFS, lcf_req_queue.py, lshare_req_queue.py=RPM, mdrr_req_queue.py), the serving engine (slora/, ~19.3k LOC Python plus CUDA/Triton kernels), workload generators (fair_bench/trace.py) and per-figure plot scripts (fair_bench/plot/).

H2_no_root.evidence: Entirely user-space. setup.py does an editable pip install that compiles one CUDA extension (slora/csrc/lora_ops.cc + slora/csrc/bgmv/*.cu) with the system nvcc; the server is a uvicorn/FastAPI process on 127.0.0.1:8000 (slora/server/api_server.py:325-326) with zmq on localhost ports (slora/server/router/manager.py:119-122). No Dockerfile, docker-compose, requirements.txt or yaml anywhere in the tree (glob returns nothing). repo_facts.json red flags list only 'big_gpu' and 'multi_gpu' - no sudo, kernel module, eBPF, perf, KVM, RDMA or CXL hits. --tp defaults to 1 (slora/server/api_server.py:341) so the S-LoRA tensor-parallel path is never entered.

H3_hardware_fit.evidence: Headline setting is ONE A10G 24GB with Llama-2-7b and a 10000-token KV pool (paper.txt:1040-1042; fair_bench/README.md:4,15) - the same class as the target RTX A5000 24GB Ampere. Weights are synthetic (--dummy hard-coded at fair_bench/launch_server.py:31), so fp16 7B ~13.5GB + 10000-token KV pool (32 layers x 2 x 4096 x 2B x 10000 ~ 5.2GB) ~ 19GB < 24GB. Repo is 34.9MB and nothing is downloaded, so ~257GB free disk is ample. Gap: the Section 5.4 ablation (Figure 15) uses Llama-2-13b on A100 80GB with 35000/65000-token pools (fair_bench/README.md:167-192, suites overload-s4-* in fair_bench/exp_suite.py:87-163); 13B fp16 (~26GB) does not fit in 24GB and needs a scale-down to 7B with two smaller pools, which still tests the 'service difference grows with M' claim. All of Sections 5.2 and 5.3 run at paper scale on one GPU.

H4_obtainable_deps_data.evidence: Deps are pip/conda-installable with no system package needed (setup.py:53-68: aiohttp, einops, fastapi, ninja, packaging, pyzmq, rpyc, safetensors, transformers, triton==2.1.0, uvloop, uvicorn, psutil; torch 2.1.2+cu118 per fair_bench/README.md:5). No model weights are downloaded: --dummy makes slora/utils/model_utils.py:6-14 read the architecture from a hard-coded table (slora/mprophet/model_config.py:49-61) and slora/models/llama/layer_weights/transformer_layer_weight.py:37-54 fills random tensors; only the public non-gated huggyllama/llama-7b tokenizer is fetched (slora/server/detokenization/manager.py:29) and prompts are 'Hello ' x N (fair_bench/trace.py:32-33). Synthetic traces are generated in-process (fair_bench/trace.py); the LMSYS Chatbot Arena trace is bundled as fair_bench/real_trace.pkl and loaded at fair_bench/run_exp.py:213-217. No proprietary data. Caveat: fair_bench/README.md:207-209 says the original trace was lost and the bundled one is resampled, so Section 5.3 numbers differ from the paper.

reproduce.target: Figure 3a (pages/page-11.png; caption paper.txt:1147-1153) - 'Absolute Difference in Service' over time for two continuously backlogged clients (90 vs 180 req/min, 256 input / 256 output), VTC vs FCFS. It supports Theorem 4.4: VTC's accumulated service difference stays bounded and independent of the interval length while FCFS's grows linearly to ~3e5 by t~500s. The same two runs also emit overload_quant_fairness.tex (plot_6.2_work_diff.py:114-134), the synthetic analogue of Table 2.
reproduce.scale_down: None required for the target. Run the AE recipe verbatim: Llama-7b dummy weights on the single A5000 24GB, --num-token 10000, suite 'overload' (fair_bench/exp_suite.py:54-64: 2 clients at 1.5 and 3 req/s, 6 min, 256 in / 256 out). If the A5000 turns out materially faster than the A10G and client 1 stops being backlogged, drop --num-token to ~8000 or raise both req_rate entries - the figure only assumes both clients exceed capacity. Separately, the Section 5.4 ablation (Figure 15) must be scaled down from Llama-2-13b/A100-80GB with pools {35000, 65000} to Llama-7b with pools {6000, 12000}, which preserves the qualitative 'bound scales with M' claim but not the absolute numbers.
reproduce.effort: ~3 person-days + ~2 GPU-hours for Figure 3a (2 x 25 min runs plus retries); ~+6 GPU-hours to add all of Section 5.2 for both schedulers, ~+9 GPU-hours for the Section 5.3 real-trace sweep (VTC, FCFS, LCF, RPM x4).
reproduce.rationale: fair_bench/README.md:14-199 gives per-figure launch_server.py + run_exp.py commands with stated wall-clock costs ('around 25 mins' for the overload suite) and the exact output PDF paths; every plot script is committed (fair_bench/plot/plot_6.2_work_diff.py produces the target figure); the authors' own result files (fair_bench/all_results_overload.jsonl etc.) are committed for diffing; the hardware class is identical (24GB Ampere); and no model weights or external datasets are needed because of --dummy plus the bundled real_trace.pkl. Remaining risks are ordinary porting: the triton==2.1.0 / torch 2.1.2 / modern-transformers pin (and a contradiction between README.md:44 and fair_bench/README.md:5 about the torch version), Python must be 3.10+ despite setup.py:52 saying 3.9 (manager.py:470 uses single-arg traceback.format_exception), and a possible --num-token nudge for the throughput offset. The real-trace results are explicitly not bit-reproducible (fair_bench/README.md:207-209), which is why the synthetic Figure 3a is the right target.

addons.name: Preemptive VTC with a deficit threshold
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that bounded-deficit preemption - evicting the newest running request of the highest-counter client whenever max_i c_i - min_i c_i exceeds theta*U, refunding its uncharged output cost, and re-admitting it later - reduces the max and average service difference by at least 2x under backlogged long-request workloads, at under 10% aggregate throughput loss, compared with the paper's non-preemptive VTC.
addons.mechanism: Add select_preemption_victims(current_batch) to VTCReqQueue, called from the router loop just before generate_new_batch. The engine already has the machinery: RouterManager._filter_batch drives InferBatch.filter, which frees the victim's KV slots through MemoryManager.free. A preempted Req is pushed back to the head of self.user_req_list[adapter_dir] with output_ids reset (recompute policy) or retained (swap policy, reusing the engine's existing --swap path), and the counter is decremented by w_q * len(output_ids) for discarded tokens so the client is not billed for work that will be redone. Expose theta as a CLI flag next to --cost-func and sweep it.
addons.motivating_evidence: Appendix C.3 'Preemption' (paper.txt:3181-3206) proposes exactly this and labels it future work: 'if the difference in service is larger than a threshold, we can preempt the requests in processing and swap in requests from clients with lower counters'. Remark 4.7 (paper.txt:785-793) states the fairness-vs-work-conservation trade-off; Theorem 4.8 (paper.txt:800-808) only lower-bounds NON-preemptive work-conserving schedulers, so a preemptive scheduler is allowed to beat w_q*M. Figure 15b (paper.txt:1704-1767) shows the discrepancy growing with request length until the bound saturates - precisely the regime preemption should fix.
addons.feasibility_rationale: The scheduling logic itself is small, but the change is cross-cutting: it touches the request queue, the async router loop, the RPC boundary to the model process, and the per-rank InferBatch, and correctness under concurrent prefill/decode is fiddly. Evaluation reuses the existing harness and plotting and fits in roughly 10 GPU-hours (theta sweep across the overload, poisson_short_long_2 and real suites), so it is doable by 2-4 students in 10 weeks but is not a localized edit.
addons.research_value_rationale: This is the paper's own top-listed open question, and the theory says something non-trivial is at stake because the 2x-tightness result of Theorem 4.8 explicitly does not cover preemptive schedulers. Either outcome teaches something a reviewer at the original venue would want: a tighter achievable bound, or a demonstration that recompute/swap costs swamp the fairness gain on a single 24GB GPU.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'VTC fairness LLM serving preemption swap-out tighter fairness bound work-conserving tradeoff', 'preemption fair scheduling LLM serving KV cache fairness bound 2025'. Closest work: FastSwitch, https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.18424 - optimizes context-switching EFFICIENCY (I/O utilization, KV-cache granularity, multi-turn retransmission) for fairness-aware serving on vLLM; it makes preemption cheap but does not study the fairness-bound / work-conservation trade-off curve framed by VTC's Theorems 4.4 and 4.8. Also adjacent: FairBatching, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.14392 (prefill-vs-decode resource fairness, not inter-client bounds). A project must position against FastSwitch explicitly and would do well to adopt its swap mechanics as a baseline.

addons.name: KV-cache-occupancy (memory-time) service cost
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that charging clients for KV-cache occupancy over time (token-seconds resident) in addition to tokens processed improves aggregate throughput and the p95 first-token latency of short-context clients at equal measured service difference, compared with the paper's linear and profiled cost functions, under a workload mixing long-context and short-context clients.
addons.mechanism: Add a third branch 'memtime' to the cost_func dispatch. Where the 'linear' branch adds w_q per running request per decode step (vtc_req_queue.py:146-147), 'memtime' adds w_q + lambda*(req.input_len + len(req.output_ids)), i.e. a charge proportional to the KV footprint the request is holding, accrued every step it stays resident - turning the counter into a memory-time account rather than a token account (the LLM-serving analogue of dominant-resource fairness). Wire the option through get_scheduler (manager.py:37-82) and both CLIs, and add a mixed-context suite (client A 64/64, client B 768/768, both backlogged) to exp_suite.py. Sweep lambda and compare the throughput / service-difference Pareto curve against 'linear' and 'profile'.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 3.1 concedes that neither token counts nor FLOPs 'accurately reflect the actual LLM serving cost' (paper.txt:509-514). Appendix B.2 explicitly defers the choice: 'our goal is not to determine the optimal cost function or pricing model ... The investigation into the cost function and pricing model is designated for future research' (paper.txt:2645-2651). Section 2.3 explains that server capacity varies precisely because long contexts consume the memory pool (paper.txt:378-390, Figure 2). Yet the profiled h(n_p,n_q) at slora/server/router/req_queue.py:107-110 charges only at token-production time, so a request sitting in the batch holding 768 KV slots while emitting one token per step is billed the same as a 64-token request - the externality the paper itself identifies is never charged.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Localized: one new branch in two or three queue classes (well under 300 LOC), one new workload suite, and full reuse of the existing metric and plotting pipeline (fair_bench/plot/plot_6.2_work_diff.py already computes max/avg service difference and emits the LaTeX table). Fits the 24GB GPU at paper scale; roughly 4 GPU-hours for a lambda sweep across three cost functions.
addons.research_value_rationale: A natural and fairly expected refinement - most reviewers would guess the direction of the result - but it answers a question the paper explicitly left open, and producing the throughput/fairness Pareto curve across three cost functions on one harness is a solid, quotable contribution. It is not a new mechanism, which caps the interest.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'multi-resource fairness LLM serving KV cache occupancy dominant resource fairness scheduler 2025', 'memory-time fair share LLM serving'. Equinox, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16646, adds a 'Resource Fairness Counter' measuring throughput and GPU utilization alongside a user-facing counter and reports up to 1.3x throughput and 13% higher fairness versus VTC - overlapping in spirit but a different construction (Equinox's counter is prediction-driven and operator-facing; this add-on is a memory-time billing term inside VTC's own cost function h). Also adjacent: FREESH, https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.00807 (fair, resource- and energy-efficient scheduling on heterogeneous GPUs). A project must baseline against Equinox's published numbers or explain why it cannot.

addons.name: Sybil-resilient hierarchical VTC (client-identity splitting and rotation)
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a tenant which splits its traffic across k client identities obtains roughly k/(n+k-1) of server capacity under VTC instead of 1/n - breaking the isolation property of Section 3.2 - and that a two-level hierarchical VTC (tenant counter over per-identity sub-counters) restores the 1/n share with under 5% throughput loss and no degradation of the Theorem 4.4 bound among honest tenants.
addons.mechanism: Attack side: extend fair_bench/trace.py with a generator that emits one logical client's request stream under k distinct adapter_dir labels - client identity is fully client-supplied (run_exp.py puts lora_dir in the request body) and VTCReqQueue.append (:38-41) creates a fresh counter for any unseen label. A second variant rotates identities: because the counter lift at vtc_req_queue.py:44-50 sets a newcomer's counter to min{c_i} over active clients, retiring an identity and registering a fresh one resets accumulated debt to the active minimum. Defence side: add HVTCReqQueue maintaining tenant_served[t] alongside served[client]; selection picks argmin_t tenant_served[t] then argmin over that tenant's clients; both levels are charged at admission and per decode step, and the lift is applied at both levels. Register it in get_scheduler and add an n x k sweep suite.
addons.motivating_evidence: All of the paper's guarantees are stated per client and are explicit functions of n: Theorem 4.11's latency bound is 2(n-1)U/a (paper.txt:857-864) and Theorem 4.13 requires a client to stay under T/n - 5U (paper.txt:875-885). Section 3.2 claims 'a misbehaving client cannot deny the service to other clients, no matter how many requests it sends' (paper.txt:546-548) - which says nothing about how many IDENTITIES it uses. Appendix C.3 mentions hierarchical fair sharing only for the distributed multi-replica case (paper.txt:3207-3219), never as an anti-abuse mechanism. In the artifact, client identity is entirely client-supplied, so the attack is a small change to the load generator.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Both the attack workload and the hierarchical queue are small, self-contained changes (well under 500 LOC total) sitting on top of an existing per-figure evaluation harness whose metrics (max/avg service difference, per-client received service, throughput) are already computed by the committed plot scripts. Roughly 4 GPU-hours for an n x k sweep on the overload and real suites. Clearly inside 10 weeks for 2-4 students. Minor caveat: self.served and self.user_req_list are never reclaimed (vtc_req_queue.py:21-22) and the served dict is copied every batch-formation opportunity (:103), so large k needs a look at scheduler overhead.
addons.research_value_rationale: It attacks the load-bearing mechanism of an OSDI paper - the counter lift at vtc_req_queue.py:44-50 - in a regime the paper never considers, and both outcomes are informative: either the attack is devastating and hierarchical counters are a necessary amendment to the isolation claim, or the lift turns out more robust than it looks and the paper's guarantee survives with a sharper statement. Honest caveat to state in the write-up: per-flow-versus-per-aggregate gaming is a known issue in packet fair queueing, so the novelty is the LLM-serving instantiation, the measurement and the interaction with the counter lift, not the concept itself.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'strategic clients sybil identity splitting gaming fair queueing LLM serving VTC multi-tenant hierarchical', 'strategic clients fair LLM serving abuse'. Nothing found that studies identity manipulation against VTC or any LLM-serving fair scheduler; the only Sybil hits were blockchain-consensus papers (e.g. FairWave). The closest adjacent follow-up, Locality-aware Fair Scheduling / DLPM and D2LPM by the same group, https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.14312, changes the ORDERING policy (prefix locality) and keeps the per-client identity model unchanged.

addons.name: Predictor poisoning in VTC-with-length-prediction, and a conservative predictor
addons.hypothesis: We hypothesize that a client which shapes its own output-length pattern (a burst of very short requests followed by long ones) inflates its received service under VTC(predict) relative to plain VTC by a measurable margin, and that replacing the running mean with a high-quantile (pessimistic) estimator removes most of that gain while retaining the bulk of VTC(predict)'s service-discrepancy reduction.
addons.mechanism: The shipped predictor is a per-client exponentially-weighted mean of that client's own recent output lengths (vtc_pred_len_req_queue.py:180-187); the predicted cost is charged up front at admission (:126-136) and reconciled downward on completion (:167-178). Because the client sets max_new_tokens with ignore_eos (fair_bench/run_exp.py), it controls its own predictor. (a) Add an adversarial generator to fair_bench/trace.py that alternates short-burst and long-burst phases per client with a tunable period and amplitude. (b) Replace the mean with a windowed q-quantile over the last W completions, plus a 'no refund on over-prediction' variant, exposed as CLI knobs. Measure received service, max/avg service difference and throughput for {VTC, VTC(predict), VTC(quantile), VTC(oracle)} - the same four-way comparison the authors already script in fair_bench/REVISION.md.
addons.motivating_evidence: Section 4.4 (paper.txt:962-988) motivates prediction purely as a variance reducer and notes 'the effectiveness of the length predictor is contingent upon both the workload and the accuracy of predictions', but every evaluation of it (Figure 19, Tables 5 and 6 at paper.txt:2744-2782) uses stationary per-client length distributions or a synthetic +/-50% error model - never an adversarial or shifting one. The Section 5.2 'distribution shift' experiment (Figure 10, paper.txt:1367-1456) shifts request RATES, not lengths, and is run against plain VTC and LCF. Theorem 4.8 says the worst case does not improve with prediction, so the prediction variant is a purely heuristic average-case gain whose robustness is untested.
addons.feasibility_rationale: Both the adversarial generator and the quantile predictor are small, localized edits to files that already exist and are already wired into the CLI (--scheduler vtc_len_predict, --predict-range). The AE REVISION.md recipe already runs exactly this four-way comparison, so only a new suite in exp_suite.py is needed. Roughly 4 GPU-hours; fits the 24GB GPU at paper scale.
addons.research_value_rationale: A narrow but real robustness question about a component the paper ships and recommends, and the finding would generalize to every prediction-based fair scheduler (including Equinox's MoPE predictor). It introduces no new mechanism beyond swapping an estimator, which caps how much a reviewer at the original venue would care.

scoop_check.details: Queries: 'output length prediction fairness scheduler VTC service discrepancy learned predictor LLM serving', 'uncertainty-aware output length prediction LLM scheduling'. Equinox, https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.16646, replaces VTC's naive predictor with a deterministic mixture-of-prediction-experts framework (L1 error on output tokens 80 -> 33) for fairness scheduling, so 'better predictor for fair scheduling' is taken. The adversarial self-poisoning angle and the conservative-quantile defence are not covered, and Equinox's predictor would be subject to the same attack. Scheduling LLM Inference with Uncertainty-Aware Output Length Predictions, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.00499, targets SJF-style scheduling rather than fairness.

risks: Implementation deviates from Algorithm 2 in the whole-system-idle case: VTCReqQueue.append (slora/server/router/vtc_req_queue.py:44-50) implements only the 'Q non-empty' branch of the counter lift (Alg. 2 lines 11-13). Lines 8-10 - 'if Q is empty, let l be the last client that left Q, set c_u <- max{c_u, c_l}' (paper.txt:640-646) - have no counterpart: when no other client has a non-empty per-client deque, cnts is empty and NO lift happens. This matters for the ON/OFF and dist-shift experiments (Figures 5, 6, 10) where the system can drain, and it is the same code path AO3's rotation attack exploits. A reproduction should check whether the shipped behaviour still yields the paper's plots.

Per-client scheduler state is never reclaimed: self.served and self.user_req_list (vtc_req_queue.py:21-22, 38-43) grow monotonically with the number of distinct adapter_dir labels, and generate_new_batch copies the whole served dict on every batch-formation opportunity (:103). Harmless at 2-27 clients, a scalability concern for AO3's k-identity sweeps.

Real-trace results are not bit-reproducible by the authors' own admission: fair_bench/README.md:207-209 states the original Chatbot Arena trace was lost and the bundled real_trace.pkl is resampled from a different time range, so Table 2 and Figures 12-14 will differ. Any claim about Section 5.3 must be phrased at trend level.

Dependency archaeology: triton==2.1.0 (setup.py:64) pins the stack to torch 2.1.x / cu118. The top-level README.md:44 ('1.13 <= PyTorch <= 2.0.1') contradicts fair_bench/README.md:5 ('PyTorch 2.1.2'); the fair_bench number is the one to trust for the VTC experiments. transformers is unpinned and a modern version may break the Llama tokenizer path (slora/server/tokenizer.py, fair_bench/trace.py). Not fatal, but the most likely place the first week goes.

Python version floor is higher than advertised: setup.py:52 says >=3.9 but slora/server/router/manager.py:470 uses the single-argument traceback.format_exception(e) form, which is 3.10+. It only fires on the error path, i.e. exactly when something else has already gone wrong - use Python 3.10.

Throughput offset A5000 vs A10G: the synthetic suites hard-code request rates chosen so that clients are backlogged on an A10G (fair_bench/exp_suite.py:54-64). If the A5000 is materially faster, 'backlogged' may no longer hold and Figure 3a's premise breaks. Verify from the server log line 'current batch size ... token used ratio' (manager.py:201) that the queue never drains, and adjust --num-token or req_rate if it does.

Figure numbering drift between the arXiv version the artifact targets and the USENIX version used here: the AE README's 'Figure 14' is USENIX Figure 15, its 'Figure 11/12/13' are USENIX 12/13/14, and plot filenames say sec6.2 where the paper says Section 5.2. Cheap to trip over when hunting for an apparently missing script.

Crowded follow-up space since 2024: DLPM/D2LPM (locality + fairness, same group, arXiv 2501.14312), FastSwitch (preemption efficiency, arXiv 2411.18424), Equinox (prediction + resource counters, arXiv 2508.16646), FairBatching (prefill/decode fairness, arXiv 2510.14392). Any add-on must be positioned against these; the least-covered angles found were AO3 (identity manipulation) and AO4's adversarial framing.

The Section 5.4 ablation scale-down changes the quantity being varied: reproducing Figure 15 at 7B with pools {6000, 12000} instead of 13B with {35000, 65000} preserves the qualitative 'bound scales with M' claim but not the absolute numbers, and must be presented as such rather than as a match.

Artifact badges could not be confirmed: the USENIX presentation page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher and search found no badge listing, so the 'Results Reproduced' style evidence that would further de-risk the reproduction estimate is absent - the H rating rests on the AE instructions, committed result files and hardware match instead.
